**# Extension AI Guard — System Architecture**



**## 1. Project Overview**



**Extension AI Guard is an AI-powered browser extension security platform designed to analyze network traffic generated by browser extensions.**



**The system captures network traffic from a controlled browser-extension testing environment, processes the captured packet and flow data, extracts relevant network features, and uses a trained machine-learning model to determine whether the observed behavior is benign or suspicious.**



**The platform is designed for both technical and non-technical users. An AI Security Assistant guides first-time users through the testing process and explains the analysis results in simple language, while Analyst and Research modes provide deeper technical and machine-learning information.**



**The system will also include a controlled extension laboratory, classical machine-learning models, experimental Quantum Machine Learning, real-time detection, a security dashboard, automated n8n workflows, and Telegram notifications.**



**### Core Principle**



**The ML model analyzes \*\*network-traffic features\*\*, not the source code of the browser extension.**



**The primary detection pipeline is:**



**Browser Extension → Network Traffic → Packet Capture → Flow Processing → Feature Extraction → ML Model → Risk Classification → Explanation / Alert**



**## 2. Problem Definition**



**Browser extensions can generate network traffic in the background while users may not understand what the extension is communicating with or whether its network behavior is normal.**



**Traditional users generally cannot inspect packet-level information or determine whether observed network activity represents legitimate or suspicious behavior.**



**Extension AI Guard addresses this problem by providing a controlled environment where browser-extension network traffic can be captured, processed, analyzed, and classified using a machine-learning model.**



**The system converts complex network-traffic information into understandable security results so that both normal users and security analysts can investigate extension behavior.**



**## 3. Project Objectives**



**The main objectives of Extension AI Guard are:**



**1. Build a controlled browser-extension testing laboratory.**



**2. Develop our own benign extension and controlled suspicious-traffic simulator for generating reproducible training and testing traffic.**



**3. Capture network traffic generated during extension testing using packet-capture tools.**



**4. Process packet captures into structured network flows.**



**5. Extract meaningful statistical and network-behavior features from the captured traffic.**



**6. Generate a labeled dataset from our controlled benign and suspicious traffic.**



**7. Train and evaluate machine-learning models for network-behavior classification.**



**8. Compare multiple classical machine-learning algorithms and select a suitable model based on measured performance.**



**9. Experiment with Quantum Machine Learning as a research comparison with classical approaches.**



**10. Integrate the trained model into a detection pipeline.**



**11. Provide real-time or near-real-time analysis of supported test traffic.**



**12. Build a secure backend for authentication, testing, detection history, and reporting.**



**13. Provide a professional security dashboard for beginner, analyst, and research users.**



**14. Provide an AI Security Assistant that guides first-time users and explains detection results.**



**15. Integrate n8n and Telegram for configurable automated security notifications.**



**16. Apply security controls, testing, documentation, and deployment practices throughout the project.**



**## 4. System Users and Roles**



**Extension AI Guard is designed to support users with different levels of technical knowledge.**



**### 4.1 Beginner User**



**The Beginner User is a normal user who may not have cybersecurity or network-analysis knowledge.**



**The system provides:**



**- Simple login and authentication.**

**- AI-guided onboarding.**

**- Step-by-step testing instructions.**

**- Simple security results.**

**- Risk levels such as Low, Medium, and High.**

**- Human-readable explanations.**

**- Basic detection history.**



**The Beginner User does not need to understand packets, protocols, or machine-learning models to use the platform.**



**### 4.2 Security Analyst**



**The Security Analyst can investigate extension behavior in greater technical detail.**



**The analyst can access:**



**- Network-flow information.**

**- Packet statistics.**

**- Destination information.**

**- Extracted traffic features.**

**- Detection results.**

**- Model confidence.**

**- Test history.**

**- Analysis reports.**

**- PCAP references from the controlled testing environment.**



**### 4.3 Research User**



**The Research User is intended for studying the machine-learning and Quantum Machine Learning components.**



**The research interface can provide:**



**- Dataset information.**

**- Feature information.**

**- Training results.**

**- Model evaluation metrics.**

**- Classical ML comparison.**

**- Quantum ML experimental results.**

**- Classical-versus-quantum analysis.**

**- Research reports.**



**### 4.4 Administrator**



**The Administrator manages the platform and its configuration.**



**Administrator capabilities may include:**



**- User and role management.**

**- System configuration.**

**- Test-environment management.**

**- Monitoring system health.**

**- Reviewing audit events.**

**- Managing alert configuration.**



**Administrative functionality will be restricted using role-based access control.**



**### Role Separation**



**The system will follow the principle of least privilege.**



**Users will only receive access to the features and information required for their role.**



**The final authorization design will be implemented using secure backend controls rather than relying only on frontend visibility.**



**## 5. End-to-End System Workflow**



**The Extension AI Guard workflow consists of multiple stages, beginning with user authentication and ending with a security decision and optional alert.**



**### 5.1 User Authentication**



**The user first accesses the Extension AI Guard web application and authenticates using the available authentication mechanism.**



**After successful authentication, the system determines the user's role and provides access to the appropriate features.**



**### 5.2 AI-Guided Onboarding**



**For a first-time user, the AI Security Assistant explains:**



**- What Extension AI Guard does.**

**- What the extension testing process involves.**

**- How to select a test extension.**

**- How to start a controlled analysis.**

**- How to understand the final security result.**



**The assistant is designed to reduce the technical knowledge required to perform the first analysis.**



**### 5.3 Extension Selection**



**The user selects an extension from the controlled Extension AI Guard testing laboratory.**



**The laboratory contains:**



**- A benign extension used to generate normal baseline traffic.**

**- A controlled suspicious-traffic simulator used to generate predefined suspicious network behavior.**



**The extensions are tested only within the controlled project environment.**



**### 5.4 Controlled Traffic Generation**



**The selected extension performs its predefined activities against the project's controlled test infrastructure.**



**The generated network activity becomes the input for the traffic-capture stage.**



**### 5.5 Network Traffic Capture**



**Network traffic generated during the test is captured using tools such as TShark or Wireshark.**



**The capture process produces PCAP data that represents the observed network communication.**



**### 5.6 Packet and Flow Processing**



**The captured PCAP data is processed to obtain structured information.**



**The processing stage identifies relevant packets and groups network activity into flows or sessions where appropriate.**



**The system then calculates measurable characteristics from the observed traffic.**



**### 5.7 Feature Extraction**



**The processed traffic is converted into machine-learning features.**



**Potential features include:**



**- Packet count.**

**- Flow duration.**

**- Total bytes transferred.**

**- Packet-size statistics.**

**- Packet timing and inter-arrival statistics.**

**- Connection frequency.**

**- Protocol and port information.**

**- Destination-related characteristics.**

**- Domain-related statistical characteristics.**



**The final feature set will be determined through experimentation and validation during implementation.**



**### 5.8 ML Analysis**



**The extracted features are passed to the trained machine-learning model.**



**The model evaluates the observed traffic and produces a classification and associated confidence or risk information.**



**The initial classification categories will be defined during dataset creation and model development.**



**### 5.9 Risk Assessment**



**The detection engine converts the model output into a user-facing security result.**



**The result may include:**



**- Classification.**

**- Risk level.**

**- Model confidence.**

**- Important contributing traffic characteristics.**

**- Test information.**



**### 5.10 Result Explanation**



**The system presents the result differently depending on the user's role.**



**A beginner receives a simple explanation through the dashboard and AI Security Assistant.**



**An analyst can inspect technical traffic and feature information.**



**A research user can inspect model and experimental information.**



**### 5.11 Alert Generation**



**If a configured detection condition is met, the detection engine can send the event to the automation layer.**



**The automation workflow uses n8n to process the event and can send a notification through the Telegram Bot integration.**



**### 5.12 Detection History**



**The system stores appropriate application-level test and detection information so users can review previous analyses according to their permissions.**



**The system will avoid storing unnecessary sensitive traffic information in the application database.**



**### Overall Workflow**



**The complete workflow can be summarized as:**



**User Authentication**

**→ AI Onboarding**

**→ Extension Selection**

**→ Controlled Traffic Generation**

**→ Network Traffic Capture**

**→ PCAP Processing**

**→ Flow Processing**

**→ Feature Extraction**

**→ ML Analysis**

**→ Risk Assessment**

**→ Result Explanation**

**→ Optional Alert**

**→ Detection History**



**## 6. Component Architecture**



**Extension AI Guard is divided into separate components so that each part of the system has a clear responsibility.**



**### 6.1 Frontend**



**The frontend provides the web interface through which users interact with Extension AI Guard.**



**Responsibilities include:**



**- User registration and login interface.**

**- Role-based navigation.**

**- AI onboarding interface.**

**- Extension testing interface.**

**- Test status and progress display.**

**- Security results.**

**- Detection history.**

**- Analyst views.**

**- Research views.**

**- Security dashboards.**

**- Reports and visualizations.**



**The frontend communicates with the backend through authenticated API requests.**



**### 6.2 Backend**



**The backend provides the central application and API layer.**



**Responsibilities include:**



**- Authentication and authorization.**

**- User and role management.**

**- Test management.**

**- Communication with the ML inference engine.**

**- Detection-result management.**

**- Detection history.**

**- Report generation.**

**- Alert-event processing.**

**- Secure communication between application components.**



**FastAPI will be used as the initial backend framework.**



**### 6.3 Browser Extension Laboratory**



**The extension laboratory provides controlled extensions for generating reproducible network behavior.**



**The laboratory will contain:**



**- Benign Extension.**

**- Controlled Suspicious-Traffic Simulator.**



**The extensions will be developed specifically for this project and tested within the controlled environment.**



**### 6.4 Traffic Capture Layer**



**The traffic layer is responsible for observing network communication generated during controlled extension tests.**



**Planned tools include:**



**- TShark.**

**- Wireshark.**

**- Scapy where appropriate.**



**The layer produces packet-capture data and related processing information for the analysis pipeline.**



**### 6.5 Packet and Flow Processing**



**This component converts raw packet captures into structured network information.**



**Responsibilities include:**



**- Reading PCAP data.**

**- Extracting packet-level information.**

**- Grouping packets into flows where appropriate.**

**- Calculating flow statistics.**

**- Preparing structured records for feature engineering.**



**### 6.6 Machine Learning Layer**



**The ML layer is responsible for creating and running the project's trained detection models.**



**Responsibilities include:**



**- Dataset preparation.**

**- Feature preprocessing.**

**- Model training.**

**- Model comparison.**

**- Model evaluation.**

**- Model serialization.**

**- Inference on new traffic features.**



**Initial classical models will include Random Forest and XGBoost.**



**### 6.7 Quantum ML Research Layer**



**The Quantum ML component is an experimental research layer.**



**It will investigate approaches such as:**



**- Variational Quantum Classifiers.**

**- Quantum Support Vector Machine approaches.**



**Quantum models will be evaluated against compatible classical baselines using measured experimental results.**



**The quantum component is not required for the basic detection pipeline to operate.**



**### 6.8 Model Storage**



**The model-storage component maintains trained model artifacts required for inference.**



**The project will distinguish between:**



**- Source code.**

**- Training datasets.**

**- Model artifacts.**

**- Configuration.**

**- Secrets.**



**Large or sensitive artifacts will not automatically be committed to the public Git repository.**



**### 6.9 Data Layer**



**The data component manages project datasets and structured application data.**



**It will distinguish between:**



**- Raw controlled traffic data.**

**- Processed traffic data.**

**- Feature datasets.**

**- Training data.**

**- Test data.**

**- Application records.**



**Data-handling rules will be defined before collecting real test data.**



**### 6.10 Automation and Alerting**



**The automation component connects detection events to external notification workflows.**



**Planned architecture:**



**Detection Engine**

**→ Backend Event**

**→ n8n Workflow**

**→ Telegram Notification**



**The automation layer will only receive the information required for the configured notification.**



**### 6.11 Testing Layer**



**The testing component validates each major part of the system.**



**Testing will cover:**



**- Backend APIs.**

**- Authentication.**

**- Authorization.**

**- Extension behavior.**

**- Traffic capture.**

**- Packet processing.**

**- Feature extraction.**

**- ML inference.**

**- Dashboard functionality.**

**- Automation.**

**- End-to-end workflows.**



**### 6.12 Documentation Layer**



**The documentation component records the project's technical design and implementation decisions.**



**Important documentation will include:**



**- Architecture.**

**- Threat model.**

**- Data flow.**

**- User flow.**

**- ML methodology.**

**- Dataset methodology.**

**- API design.**

**- Security design.**

**- Testing methodology.**

**- Deployment procedure.**



**### Component Relationship**



**The major components interact as follows:**



**Frontend**

**→ Backend API**

**→ Testing and Detection Services**

**→ Traffic Processing**

**→ Feature Engineering**

**→ ML Inference**

**→ Detection Result**

**→ Dashboard**



**The Backend also communicates with:**



**Backend**

**→ Database**



**Detection Engine**

**→ Automation**

**→ Telegram**



**Research Pipeline**

**→ Quantum ML**

**→ Experimental Evaluation**



**## 7. Data Flow Architecture**



**The data flow describes how network-traffic information moves through Extension AI Guard from the controlled browser-extension environment to the final security result.**



**### 7.1 High-Level Data Flow**



**The primary data flow is:**



**Controlled Extension**

**→ Network Activity**

**→ Packet Capture**

**→ PCAP**

**→ Packet Processing**

**→ Flow Construction**

**→ Feature Extraction**

**→ Preprocessing**

**→ ML Inference**

**→ Risk Classification**

**→ Dashboard / AI Explanation**

**→ Optional Alert**



**### 7.2 Stage 1 — Extension Activity**



**A user starts a controlled extension test through the Extension AI Guard application.**



**The selected extension performs its predefined activities within the testing environment.**



**The system records the test identifier and relevant test metadata.**



**### 7.3 Stage 2 — Network Traffic**



**The extension generates network requests during its controlled activities.**



**The resulting communication becomes the raw input for the traffic-capture component.**



**### 7.4 Stage 3 — Packet Capture**



**The traffic-capture component observes the network communication and produces a PCAP file.**



**The PCAP represents the packets observed during the test.**



**The capture process will be isolated to the controlled testing environment.**



**### 7.5 Stage 4 — Packet Processing**



**The packet-processing component reads the PCAP and extracts structured packet information.**



**Example information includes:**



**- Timestamp.**

**- Source and destination information.**

**- Protocol.**

**- Source and destination port where available.**

**- Packet length.**

**- Packet timing information.**



**### 7.6 Stage 5 — Flow Construction**



**Packets belonging to related network communication are grouped into flows where appropriate.**



**Flow-level records can contain information such as:**



**- Flow duration.**

**- Number of packets.**

**- Bytes transferred.**

**- Packet-size statistics.**

**- Timing statistics.**

**- Directional traffic statistics.**



**### 7.7 Stage 6 — Feature Engineering**



**The system transforms processed flow information into numerical features suitable for machine-learning models.**



**The feature-engineering stage is responsible for ensuring that the same feature definitions are used consistently during training and inference.**



**The final feature list will be determined experimentally using the project's controlled dataset.**



**### 7.8 Stage 7 — Preprocessing**



**The extracted features are passed through the same preprocessing procedure used during model training.**



**Depending on the selected model and feature set, preprocessing may include:**



**- Missing-value handling.**

**- Data-type validation.**

**- Feature transformation.**

**- Scaling where required.**

**- Feature selection.**



**Training and inference preprocessing must remain consistent.**



**### 7.9 Stage 8 — ML Inference**



**The processed feature vector is provided to the trained machine-learning model.**



**The model produces a classification and, where supported, a probability or confidence-related output.**



**The inference service does not retrain the model during normal detection.**



**### 7.10 Stage 9 — Risk Classification**



**The detection engine converts the model output into a standardized security result.**



**The result can contain:**



**- Test ID.**

**- Classification.**

**- Risk level.**

**- Model output.**

**- Confidence or probability information where available.**

**- Relevant feature information.**

**- Timestamp.**



**### 7.11 Stage 10 — User Presentation**



**The detection result is returned to the frontend.**



**The dashboard presents the result according to the user's role.**



**Beginner users receive a simplified explanation.**



**Security analysts receive detailed traffic and feature information.**



**Research users receive additional model and experimental information.**



**### 7.12 Stage 11 — AI Explanation**



**The AI Security Assistant can use the detection result and approved analysis information to explain the result in understandable language.**



**The assistant is an explanation and onboarding layer.**



**The underlying ML model remains responsible for the actual classification.**



**### 7.13 Stage 12 — Automated Alert**



**When the configured alert condition is satisfied, the detection event can be passed to the automation layer.**



**The workflow becomes:**



**Detection Engine**

**→ n8n**

**→ Telegram Bot**

**→ User Notification**



**### 7.14 Training Data Flow**



**The training pipeline is separate from normal inference.**



**The training flow is:**



**Controlled Benign Extension**

**→ Benign Traffic**

**→ PCAP**

**→ Processing**

**→ Features**

**→ Benign Label**



**Controlled Suspicious-Traffic Simulator**

**→ Suspicious Traffic**

**→ PCAP**

**→ Processing**

**→ Features**

**→ Suspicious Label**



**The resulting records are combined into a labeled dataset.**



**The dataset is then:**



**Dataset**

**→ Preprocessing**

**→ Train/Test Split**

**→ Model Training**

**→ Evaluation**

**→ Model Selection**

**→ Model Serialization**



**### 7.15 Training and Inference Separation**



**Training and inference are separate processes.**



**Training is performed during the model-development stage.**



**After a model has been evaluated and selected, the trained artifact is used by the inference engine.**



**This prevents normal user testing from unexpectedly changing the trained model.**



**### 7.16 Data Protection**



**The system will minimize unnecessary storage of captured network information.**



**Sensitive configuration values and credentials will be stored outside source code.**



**Public Git repositories will not contain:**



**- API keys.**

**- Passwords.**

**- Authentication secrets.**

**- Private credentials.**

**- Unnecessary raw network captures.**



**Data-retention rules will be defined during implementation and deployment.**



**### Complete Data Flow**



**The complete detection path is:**



**Extension**

**→ Network Traffic**

**→ TShark/Wireshark**

**→ PCAP**

**→ Packet Processing**

**→ Flow Processing**

**→ Feature Engineering**

**→ Preprocessing**

**→ Trained ML Model**

**→ Detection Engine**

**→ Risk Result**

**→ Dashboard**

**→ AI Explanation**

**→ Optional n8n/Telegram Alert**



**## 8. Machine Learning Architecture**



**The Machine Learning component is the core intelligence layer of Extension AI Guard.**



**The ML system will be trained using traffic generated from the project's own controlled browser-extension laboratory.**



**The model will not directly analyze browser-extension source code. Instead, it will learn patterns from structured network-traffic features extracted from controlled traffic captures.**



**### 8.1 ML Pipeline**



**The overall ML pipeline is:**



**Controlled Extensions**

**→ Traffic Generation**

**→ PCAP Capture**

**→ Packet Processing**

**→ Flow Construction**

**→ Feature Engineering**

**→ Dataset Creation**

**→ Data Preprocessing**

**→ Train/Test Split**

**→ Model Training**

**→ Model Evaluation**

**→ Model Selection**

**→ Model Serialization**

**→ Inference**



**### 8.2 Dataset Generation**



**The project will generate its own dataset using controlled extensions.**



**Two primary traffic categories will initially be created:**



**- Benign traffic.**

**- Suspicious traffic.**



**The benign extension will generate normal baseline network activity.**



**The controlled suspicious-traffic simulator will generate predefined suspicious network behavior within the isolated test environment.**



**Each generated traffic sample will be associated with an appropriate label.**



**The dataset will therefore be derived from reproducible project-controlled experiments rather than relying entirely on an externally downloaded dataset.**



**### 8.3 Dataset Structure**



**Each processed traffic record will contain:**



**- A test or flow identifier.**

**- Extracted network features.**

**- The corresponding class label.**

**- Required metadata for experiment tracking.**



**A simplified representation is:**



**Feature 1 | Feature 2 | Feature 3 | ... | Feature N | Label**



**The exact schema will be finalized after the traffic-processing and feature-engineering stages are implemented.**



**### 8.4 Candidate Network Features**



**The initial feature candidates will be derived from measurable network-flow characteristics.**



**Potential features include:**



**- Packet count.**

**- Total bytes.**

**- Flow duration.**

**- Average packet size.**

**- Minimum and maximum packet size.**

**- Packet-size variability.**

**- Packet inter-arrival statistics.**

**- Connection frequency.**

**- Directional packet statistics.**

**- Directional byte statistics.**

**- Protocol information.**

**- Port information.**

**- Destination-related statistics.**

**- Domain-related statistical characteristics where available.**



**Features will be selected based on reproducibility, availability in the controlled traffic, usefulness for classification, and experimental evaluation.**



**### 8.5 Data Preprocessing**



**Before training, the dataset will be validated and prepared.**



**The preprocessing pipeline may include:**



**- Removing invalid records.**

**- Handling missing values.**

**- Validating feature types.**

**- Removing duplicate or unsuitable samples where required.**

**- Encoding categorical information where required.**

**- Scaling numerical features when required by the selected algorithm.**

**- Selecting the final feature set.**



**The preprocessing procedure used during training will be saved and reused during inference.**



**### 8.6 Train/Test Strategy**



**The dataset will be divided into training and evaluation portions.**



**The training data will be used to learn the model parameters.**



**The test data will remain separated from the training process and will be used to estimate performance on unseen samples.**



**Where appropriate, validation or cross-validation will be used during model selection.**



**Data leakage will be avoided by ensuring that information from the evaluation set does not influence model training.**



**### 8.7 Classical ML Models**



**The initial classical machine-learning candidates are:**



**- Random Forest.**

**- XGBoost.**



**Random Forest provides a strong tree-based baseline and can provide useful feature-importance information.**



**XGBoost provides a powerful gradient-boosting approach that can model complex relationships between traffic features.**



**Additional algorithms may be considered if experimental results justify their inclusion.**



**### 8.8 Important Training Parameters**



**The project will record the important model configuration parameters used during training.**



**For Random Forest, candidate parameters include:**



**- Number of trees.**

**- Maximum tree depth.**

**- Minimum samples required for splitting.**

**- Minimum samples required at a leaf.**

**- Feature-selection strategy.**



**For XGBoost, candidate parameters include:**



**- Number of estimators.**

**- Maximum tree depth.**

**- Learning rate.**

**- Subsample ratio.**

**- Column sampling ratio.**



**The final values will not be assumed in advance. They will be selected through controlled experiments and documented with the corresponding evaluation results.**



**### 8.9 Model Evaluation**



**The models will be evaluated using multiple metrics rather than accuracy alone.**



**The evaluation will include:**



**- Accuracy.**

**- Precision.**

**- Recall.**

**- F1-score.**

**- Confusion matrix.**

**- ROC-AUC where applicable.**



**For a security detection system, particular attention will be given to false negatives because failing to identify suspicious behavior can be more significant than incorrectly flagging benign behavior.**



**However, false-positive behavior will also be measured because excessive false alarms reduce system usability.**



**### 8.10 Model Selection**



**The final model will be selected based on measured performance and practical requirements.**



**Selection factors may include:**



**- Detection performance.**

**- False-positive rate.**

**- False-negative rate.**

**- Generalization performance.**

**- Inference speed.**

**- Resource requirements.**

**- Interpretability.**

**- Deployment compatibility.**



**The project will document why the selected model was preferred over the alternatives.**



**### 8.11 Model Serialization**



**After training and evaluation, the selected model will be serialized for later inference.**



**The project may use appropriate formats such as:**



**- Joblib.**

**- ONNX.**



**The serialized model will be loaded by the inference service.**



**The exact serialization method will depend on the final model and deployment requirements.**



**### 8.12 Inference Pipeline**



**During a new controlled analysis, the inference pipeline will be:**



**New Traffic**

**→ PCAP**

**→ Packet Processing**

**→ Flow Processing**

**→ Feature Extraction**

**→ Saved Preprocessing Pipeline**

**→ Saved ML Model**

**→ Prediction**

**→ Risk Result**



**The inference pipeline must use the same feature definitions and preprocessing logic used during training.**



**### 8.13 Model Versioning**



**Each production-ready model will have a version identifier.**



**Model records will include appropriate information such as:**



**- Model name.**

**- Model version.**

**- Training dataset version.**

**- Feature-set version.**

**- Training date.**

**- Evaluation metrics.**

**- Configuration parameters.**



**This allows detection results to be associated with the model version that produced them.**



**### 8.14 Reproducibility**



**ML experiments will be reproducible wherever practical.**



**The project will record:**



**- Dataset version.**

**- Feature definitions.**

**- Preprocessing configuration.**

**- Model parameters.**

**- Random seeds where applicable.**

**- Evaluation metrics.**

**- Model version.**



**This allows the team to explain how the final model was produced.**



**### 8.15 ML Security Considerations**



**The ML pipeline will consider security risks such as:**



**- Data leakage.**

**- Incorrect labels.**

**- Highly imbalanced classes.**

**- Training-data contamination.**

**- Distribution differences between training and testing traffic.**

**- Unvalidated input features.**

**- Unexpected inference inputs.**



**The controlled traffic-generation environment will help maintain consistent and reproducible training data.**



**### 8.16 ML Output**



**The model will produce an analysis result that can contain:**



**- Predicted class.**

**- Probability or confidence information where supported.**

**- Model version.**

**- Test identifier.**

**- Relevant feature information.**



**The detection engine will then convert the model output into the standardized result presented by the dashboard.**



**## 9. Quantum Machine Learning Architecture**



**Quantum Machine Learning (QML) will be included as an experimental research component of Extension AI Guard.**



**The primary detection system will first be developed using classical machine-learning techniques. Once the classical ML pipeline is working and evaluated, a compatible feature representation will be used to investigate Quantum ML approaches.**



**The purpose of the Quantum ML component is to experimentally compare quantum-based classification approaches with classical machine-learning baselines.**



**### 9.1 Quantum ML Pipeline**



**The experimental pipeline is:**



**Processed Network Features**

**→ Feature Selection**

**→ Compatible Feature Representation**

**→ Quantum Feature Encoding**

**→ Quantum ML Model**

**→ Prediction**

**→ Evaluation**

**→ Classical vs Quantum Comparison**



**### 9.2 Quantum ML Candidates**



**The initial research candidates are:**



**- Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC).**

**- Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) or a suitable quantum-kernel approach.**



**The exact implementation will depend on the final dataset size, feature dimensionality, simulator capabilities, and available quantum-computing resources.**



**### 9.3 Feature Preparation**



**Quantum models generally cannot directly consume an unrestricted number of classical features.**



**Therefore, the feature set used for the quantum experiment may require dimensionality reduction or feature selection.**



**The project may investigate techniques such as:**



**- Feature selection.**

**- Principal Component Analysis (PCA).**

**- Other suitable dimensionality-reduction approaches.**



**The selected technique will be documented and applied consistently to the quantum experiment.**



**### 9.4 Quantum Feature Encoding**



**Selected classical network features will be mapped into a representation suitable for a quantum circuit.**



**The encoding method will be chosen according to the final feature representation and the selected QML algorithm.**



**The project will document:**



**- Number of selected features.**

**- Encoding approach.**

**- Circuit structure.**

**- Number of qubits required.**

**- Relevant circuit parameters.**



**### 9.5 Quantum Model Training**



**The quantum model will be trained using the prepared training data.**



**Training may be performed using a quantum simulator during the research stage.**



**The experiment will record appropriate parameters such as:**



**- Number of qubits.**

**- Circuit depth.**

**- Feature-encoding method.**

**- Optimizer.**

**- Number of optimization iterations.**

**- Learning configuration.**

**- Random seed where applicable.**



**Final parameter values will be determined experimentally rather than assumed in advance.**



**### 9.6 Quantum Evaluation**



**The quantum model will be evaluated using the same or appropriately comparable evaluation methodology used for the classical models.**



**Metrics may include:**



**- Accuracy.**

**- Precision.**

**- Recall.**

**- F1-score.**

**- Confusion matrix.**

**- ROC-AUC where applicable.**



**The comparison must use compatible datasets and evaluation conditions to avoid misleading conclusions.**



**### 9.7 Classical vs Quantum Comparison**



**The research component will compare the selected quantum approach with classical baselines.**



**The comparison may consider:**



**- Classification performance.**

**- Precision.**

**- Recall.**

**- F1-score.**

**- False-positive behavior.**

**- False-negative behavior.**

**- Training characteristics.**

**- Inference characteristics.**

**- Computational requirements.**



**The project will report the measured results rather than assuming that Quantum ML will outperform classical ML.**



**### 9.8 Quantum Simulator**



**The initial QML experiments will use a simulator-based environment.**



**This allows the project to develop and evaluate the quantum algorithms without requiring access to physical quantum hardware.**



**A physical quantum backend may be investigated separately if suitable access is available.**



**### 9.9 Role of Quantum ML in the Final System**



**Quantum ML is a research and comparison component.**



**The basic Extension AI Guard detection pipeline must remain functional using the validated classical ML model.**



**Therefore:**



**Classical ML**

**→ Primary Detection Capability**



**Quantum ML**

**→ Experimental Research Capability**



**This separation ensures that the application's core security functionality does not depend on the availability of quantum hardware.**



**### 9.10 Reproducibility**



**Quantum experiments will record:**



**- Dataset version.**

**- Feature-set version.**

**- Dimensionality-reduction configuration.**

**- Number of qubits.**

**- Circuit configuration.**

**- Encoding method.**

**- Optimizer.**

**- Training configuration.**

**- Evaluation metrics.**



**This information will allow the quantum experiments to be reproduced and compared with later experiments.**



**### 9.11 Expected Research Output**



**The Quantum ML component will produce a research comparison showing how the selected quantum approach performs on the project's controlled network-traffic classification problem compared with the selected classical baseline.**



**The project will clearly distinguish experimental findings from assumptions and will not claim a quantum advantage unless the experimental results support such a conclusion.**



**## 10. Security Architecture**



**Security is a core requirement of Extension AI Guard because the platform analyzes browser-extension network behavior and includes a controlled environment for generating test traffic.**



**The system will be designed so that the testing environment, analysis pipeline, application backend, and user interface have clearly defined security boundaries.**



**### 10.1 Security Principles**



**The project will follow these principles:**



**- Least privilege.**

**- Defense in depth.**

**- Secure-by-default configuration.**

**- Separation of testing and production components.**

**- Input validation.**

**- Authentication and authorization.**

**- Protection of secrets.**

**- Minimal data retention.**

**- Auditability.**

**- Controlled execution of test extensions.**



**### 10.2 Testing Environment Isolation**



**The browser-extension testing environment will be separated from normal user activity.**



**The controlled extensions will communicate with project-controlled test infrastructure rather than arbitrary external systems.**



**The suspicious-traffic simulator will contain predefined behaviors required for the project's experiments.**



**The testing environment will not be designed to perform uncontrolled malicious activity against third-party systems.**



**### 10.3 Trust Boundaries**



**The major trust boundaries are:**



**User**

**→ Frontend**



**Frontend**

**→ Backend API**



**Backend**

**→ Database**



**Backend**

**→ Detection / ML Services**



**Testing Environment**

**→ Traffic Capture**



**Detection Engine**

**→ Automation Layer**



**Automation Layer**

**→ Telegram**



**Each boundary will be treated as an untrusted interface and protected with appropriate validation and authorization.**



**### 10.4 Authentication**



**The application will require authentication for protected functionality.**



**The authentication system will support:**



**- Secure registration.**

**- Secure login.**

**- Session management.**

**- Logout.**

**- Password protection where password authentication is used.**

**- OAuth-based authentication if enabled.**

**- Appropriate token handling.**



**Authentication credentials and secrets will never be hard-coded into source code.**



**### 10.5 Authorization**



**Authentication confirms who the user is.**



**Authorization determines what the user is allowed to access.**



**The platform will use role-based access control.**



**The primary roles are:**



**- Beginner.**

**- Security Analyst.**

**- Research User.**

**- Administrator.**



**Authorization checks will be performed on the backend.**



**The frontend will not be treated as a security boundary.**



**### 10.6 API Security**



**Backend APIs will implement appropriate controls such as:**



**- Authentication checks.**

**- Authorization checks.**

**- Input validation.**

**- Request-size limits where appropriate.**

**- Rate limiting where required.**

**- Secure error handling.**

**- CORS configuration appropriate to deployment.**

**- Protection against unauthorized access to sensitive operations.**



**### 10.7 Secrets Management**



**Sensitive values will be stored through environment-based configuration or an appropriate secret-management mechanism.**



**Examples include:**



**- Database credentials.**

**- Authentication secrets.**

**- API keys.**

**- Telegram credentials.**

**- n8n credentials.**

**- OAuth secrets.**



**The `.env` file will not be committed to GitHub.**



**Only `.env.example` containing non-secret configuration names and safe example values will be maintained in the repository.**



**### 10.8 Database Security**



**The application database will use appropriate access controls.**



**Database access will be restricted according to application requirements.**



**The system will avoid exposing database credentials to the frontend.**



**Where supported by the selected database architecture, row-level or equivalent authorization controls will be used to prevent users from accessing records belonging to other users.**



**### 10.9 Traffic and PCAP Protection**



**Network captures can contain sensitive information.**



**Therefore:**



**- PCAP files will be generated only within the controlled testing environment.**

**- Raw PCAP files will not be automatically committed to the public Git repository.**

**- Access to stored captures will be restricted.**

**- Unnecessary sensitive traffic will not be collected.**

**- Retention rules will be defined during implementation.**

**- Test traffic will use controlled or synthetic information wherever possible.**



**### 10.10 ML Pipeline Security**



**The ML pipeline will validate incoming features before inference.**



**Security considerations include:**



**- Unexpected input values.**

**- Missing features.**

**- Incorrect data types.**

**- Feature-order mismatches.**

**- Invalid serialized models.**

**- Data leakage.**

**- Incorrect labels.**

**- Training-data contamination.**



**The production inference process will use a validated model artifact and the corresponding preprocessing configuration.**



**### 10.11 Extension Security**



**The project extensions will be developed specifically for controlled experiments.**



**The benign extension will provide baseline traffic.**



**The suspicious-traffic simulator will generate predefined test behavior required to evaluate the detection pipeline.**



**Extension permissions will be kept as limited as practical.**



**The test extensions will not be treated as production browser extensions.**



**### 10.12 AI Assistant Security**



**The AI Security Assistant is an onboarding and explanation component.**



**It will not independently determine whether traffic is malicious.**



**The authoritative detection result comes from the detection and ML pipeline.**



**The AI Assistant will receive only the information required to explain the result.**



**It will not be given unrestricted access to secrets, credentials, or raw sensitive system data.**



**### 10.13 Alert Security**



**The n8n and Telegram integration will be protected using appropriate credentials and access controls.**



**Alert messages will avoid exposing unnecessary sensitive information.**



**The automation workflow will validate incoming detection events before sending notifications.**



**### 10.14 Logging and Auditing**



**Security-relevant events will be logged where appropriate.**



**Potential events include:**



**- Authentication events.**

**- Authorization failures.**

**- Test execution.**

**- Detection events.**

**- Administrative actions.**

**- Configuration changes.**

**- Automation failures.**



**Logs will avoid storing passwords, authentication secrets, or unnecessary sensitive traffic content.**



**### 10.15 Secure Development**



**Security will be incorporated throughout development rather than added only at the end.**



**The development process will include:**



**Design**

**→ Threat Modeling**

**→ Implementation**

**→ Unit Testing**

**→ Security Testing**

**→ Integration Testing**

**→ End-to-End Testing**

**→ Deployment Review**



**### 10.16 Security Goal**



**The security goal of Extension AI Guard is to ensure that users can safely perform controlled browser-extension network analysis without exposing credentials, uncontrolled test activity, or unnecessary sensitive network information.**



**## 11. Technology Stack and Deployment Architecture**



**Extension AI Guard will use a modular technology stack so that the frontend, backend, traffic-analysis pipeline, machine-learning system, quantum research environment, and automation layer can be developed and tested independently.**



**### 11.1 Frontend**



**The web application will use:**



**- React.js.**

**- Tailwind CSS.**

**- Chart.js or an equivalent visualization library.**



**The frontend will provide the main user interface for authentication, onboarding, testing, detection results, dashboards, history, and research views.**



**### 11.2 Backend**



**The backend will use:**



**- Python.**

**- FastAPI.**

**- Pydantic for request and data validation.**



**FastAPI will expose authenticated APIs used by the frontend and communicate with the required application services.**



**### 11.3 Authentication**



**The authentication architecture will use secure token/session mechanisms.**



**OAuth2 and JWT-based authorization may be used depending on the final authentication implementation.**



**Authentication and authorization decisions will ultimately be enforced by the backend.**



**### 11.4 Database**



**The planned database infrastructure is:**



**- Supabase.**

**- PostgreSQL.**



**The database will store appropriate application information such as:**



**- User-related records.**

**- Roles.**

**- Test metadata.**

**- Detection results.**

**- Detection history.**

**- Model metadata.**

**- Audit information where required.**



**Large raw PCAP files will not automatically be stored inside the application database.**



**### 11.5 Browser Extension**



**The extension laboratory will use a browser extension architecture compatible with the selected browser environment.**



**The project will maintain separate controlled extensions for:**



**- Benign baseline behavior.**

**- Suspicious-traffic simulation.**



**The extension components will remain isolated from the main application wherever practical.**



**### 11.6 Traffic Analysis**



**The traffic-analysis stack will initially include:**



**- Wireshark.**

**- TShark.**

**- Scapy where appropriate.**



**These tools will support packet capture, inspection, and processing within the controlled testing environment.**



**### 11.7 Machine Learning**



**The ML stack will include:**



**- Python.**

**- Pandas.**

**- NumPy.**

**- Scikit-learn.**

**- XGBoost.**



**The initial model candidates will include:**



**- Random Forest.**

**- XGBoost.**



**Model serialization will use an appropriate format such as Joblib or ONNX depending on the final inference architecture.**



**### 11.8 Quantum ML**



**The experimental quantum layer will use:**



**- Qiskit.**

**- PennyLane where appropriate.**

**- Quantum simulators.**



**The quantum component will initially operate as a research environment and will not be required for the primary detection pipeline.**



**### 11.9 AI Security Assistant**



**The AI Security Assistant will provide:**



**- First-time-user onboarding.**

**- Step-by-step testing guidance.**

**- Security-result explanations.**

**- Technical-term explanations.**

**- Contextual help.**



**The assistant will be separated from the authoritative detection logic.**



**### 11.10 Automation**



**The automation architecture will use:**



**- n8n.**

**- Telegram Bot integration.**



**The primary flow will be:**



**Detection Event**

**→ Backend / Detection Engine**

**→ n8n Workflow**

**→ Telegram Bot**

**→ User Alert**



**### 11.11 Development Environment**



**The development environment will initially support:**



**- Windows development.**

**- Python virtual environment.**

**- Node.js and npm.**

**- Git.**

**- GitHub.**

**- Browser developer tools.**

**- Wireshark/TShark.**



**Linux-based testing environments may be used where required for traffic-analysis or deployment testing.**

**## 12. Frontend and User Journey Architecture**



**The frontend will be designed as a security-analysis platform that can be used by both beginners and experienced security users.**



**The interface will hide unnecessary technical complexity from beginner users while providing advanced information to analysts and researchers.**



**### 12.1 First-Time User Journey**



**A first-time user will follow this simplified workflow:**



**```text**

**Open Extension AI Guard**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Create Account / Login**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Welcome Screen**

&#x20;       **↓**

**AI Security Assistant**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Understand How the Platform Works**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Select Guided Test**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Select Controlled Extension**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Start Analysis**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Watch Test Progress**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Traffic Captured**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Traffic Processed**

&#x20;       **↓**

**AI/ML Detection**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Security Result**

&#x20;       **↓**

**AI Explanation**

&#x20;       **↓**

**Recommended Next Action**

**````**



**The user should not need to understand PCAP files, packet headers, network flows, or machine-learning algorithms to complete the first test.**



**### 12.2 Authentication Screen**



**The application will provide a professional authentication interface.**



**The authentication area will support:**



**\* Registration.**

**\* Login.**

**\* Logout.**

**\* Session handling.**

**\* Password recovery where applicable.**

**\* OAuth authentication where configured.**



**After successful authentication, the user will be directed to the appropriate application experience based on their role and onboarding status.**



**### 12.3 Welcome and Onboarding Screen**



**After the first successful login, the system will identify whether the user has completed onboarding.**



**A new user will be shown a welcome experience explaining:**



**\* What Extension AI Guard is.**

**\* What the user can test.**

**\* What information will be analyzed.**

**\* How long a test may take.**

**\* What the final result means.**



**The AI Security Assistant will guide the user through this process.**



**### 12.4 AI Security Assistant**



**The AI Security Assistant will act as the user's interactive guide.**



**It can explain:**



**\* What a browser extension is.**

**\* What network traffic means.**

**\* What the current testing step is doing.**

**\* Why traffic is being captured.**

**\* What a detection result means.**

**\* What technical terms mean.**

**\* What the user can do next.**



**The assistant will provide contextual help instead of displaying large amounts of technical information at once.**



**### 12.5 Guided Testing Mode**



**Beginner users will have a Guided Testing Mode.**



**The interface will present the test as a sequence of simple steps.**



**Example:**



**```text**

**Step 1 — Choose Test**

&#x20;      **↓**

**Step 2 — Choose Extension**

&#x20;      **↓**

**Step 3 — Start Test**

&#x20;      **↓**

**Step 4 — Capture Traffic**

&#x20;      **↓**

**Step 5 — Analyze Traffic**

&#x20;      **↓**

**Step 6 — View Result**

**```**



**The interface will clearly show the current step and test progress.**



**### 12.6 Extension Selection**



**The extension-selection screen will provide controlled project extensions.**



**Each extension will have a simple explanation.**



**Example:**



**```text**

**Benign Extension**

**Normal baseline behavior**

**Recommended for first test**



**Suspicious Traffic Simulator**

**Controlled suspicious behavior**

**Recommended for security demonstration**

**```**



**The system will explain the purpose of each test before execution.**



**### 12.7 Test Execution Screen**



**During testing, the frontend will show the current system state.**



**Possible states include:**



**\* Preparing test.**

**\* Starting extension.**

**\* Generating traffic.**

**\* Capturing packets.**

**\* Processing traffic.**

**\* Extracting features.**

**\* Running ML inference.**

**\* Generating result.**



**The user will not need to manually operate packet-analysis tools during the guided workflow.**



**### 12.8 Security Result Screen**



**After analysis, the user will receive a clear security result.**



**The result can include:**



**\* Overall risk level.**

**\* Classification.**

**\* Confidence or probability information where available.**

**\* Test summary.**

**\* Important traffic characteristics.**

**\* Recommended next action.**



**The interface will prioritize understandable explanations.**



**### 12.9 Beginner Result Example**



**A beginner-oriented result may follow this structure:**



**```text**

**Security Result**



**Risk Level: HIGH**



**What happened?**

**The tested extension generated network behavior that**

**matches patterns associated with suspicious traffic.**



**Why?**

**The system observed unusual traffic characteristics.**



**What should you do?**

**Review the extension and investigate the detected behavior.**



**Need help?**

**Ask the AI Security Assistant.**

**```**



**The exact wording and risk-calculation logic will be determined during implementation and validated against the detection engine.**



**### 12.10 Analyst Mode**



**Security analysts will have access to additional technical information.**



**The analyst interface may include:**



**\* Flow information.**

**\* Packet statistics.**

**\* Protocol information.**

**\* Destination information.**

**\* Feature values.**

**\* Detection confidence.**

**\* Model version.**

**\* Test metadata.**

**\* Analysis history.**



**The analyst will be able to move from a high-level result into deeper technical evidence.**



**### 12.11 Research Mode**



**Research users will have access to the ML and Quantum ML experimental information.**



**The research interface may provide:**



**\* Dataset information.**

**\* Feature sets.**

**\* Model versions.**

**\* Training results.**

**\* Evaluation metrics.**

**\* Classical ML comparisons.**

**\* Quantum ML experiment results.**

**\* Experiment history.**

**Potential dashboard sections include:**



**\* Total tests.**

**\* Risk distribution.**

**\* Recent detections.**

**\* Detection trends.**

**\* Model information.**

**\* System status.**

**\* Quick-start testing.**

**A history record may contain:**



**\* Test date and time.**

**\* Test type.**

**\* Extension identifier.**

**\* Detection result.**

**\* Risk level.**

**\* Model version.**

**\* Analysis status.**



**Sensitive raw traffic information will not be unnecessarily exposed in the standard history view.**



**### 12.14 Navigation**



**The frontend navigation will be role-aware.**



**A beginner may see:**



**```text**

**Home**

**Guided Test**

**My Results**

**History**

**AI Assistant**

**Help**

**```**

**```text**

**Traffic Analysis**

**Flow Details**

**Detection Details**

**Reports**

**```**



**A research user may additionally see:**

**ML Experiments**

**Quantum Lab**

**Comparisons**

**```**



**Administrators may additionally see:**



**```text**

**Users**

**System Configuration**

**Audit Events**

**System Health**

**```**



**### 12.15 Accessibility and Usability**



**The interface will be designed to reduce unnecessary complexity.**



**The application will aim to provide:**



**\* Clear labels.**

**\* Consistent navigation.**

**\* Understandable error messages.**

**\* Responsive layouts.**

**\* Keyboard-accessible interactions where practical.**

**\* Clear visual distinction between normal, warning, and high-risk results.**

**\* Avoidance of security decisions based only on color.**



**### 12.16 Frontend Security Boundary**



**The frontend is a user interface and is not considered a trusted security boundary.**



**Important security decisions will be performed by the backend.**



**The frontend will never be relied upon alone to enforce:**



**\* User permissions.**

**\* Role restrictions.**

**\* Access to detection records.**

**\* Administrative privileges.**

**\* Sensitive operations.**



**### 12.17 Overall User Experience Goal**

&#x20;   **↓**

&#x20;   **↓**

**## 13. Backend and API Architecture**



**The backend will act as the central application layer of Extension AI Guard.**



**It will provide secure APIs for authentication, user management, testing, traffic-analysis coordination, ML inference, detection results, history, reporting, and administrative operations.**



**The backend will initially be implemented using Python and FastAPI.**



**### 13.1 Backend Responsibilities**



**The backend will be responsible for:**



**- Authentication.**

**- Authorization.**

**- User and role management.**

**- Test creation and management.**

**- Extension-test coordination.**

**- Traffic-analysis coordination.**

**- ML inference requests.**

**- Detection-result management.**

**- Detection history.**

**- Model information.**

**- Report generation.**

**- Alert-event generation.**

**- Audit events.**

**- System configuration where permitted.**



**### 13.2 API Architecture**



**The frontend will communicate with the backend using HTTPS API requests.**



**The general communication flow is:**



**```text**

**React Frontend**

&#x20;     **↓**

**Authenticated API Request**

&#x20;     **↓**

**FastAPI Backend**

&#x20;     **↓**

**Authentication / Authorization**

&#x20;     **↓**

**Application Service**

&#x20;     **↓**

**Database / Detection Engine / Other Service**

&#x20;     **↓**

**API Response**

&#x20;     **↓**

**React Frontend**

**````**



**### 13.3 API Layer Separation**



**The backend will be organized into logical layers.**



**The planned structure is:**



**```text**

**API Routes**

&#x20;   **↓**

**Authentication / Authorization**

&#x20;   **↓**

**Service Layer**

&#x20;   **↓**

**Business Logic**

&#x20;   **↓**

**Data / External Services**

**```**



**API routes will handle HTTP communication.**



**The service layer will contain application logic.**



**Database operations and external-service communication will remain separated from route definitions where practical.**



**### 13.4 Authentication API**



**Authentication endpoints will support the configured authentication system.**



**Potential operations include:**



**```text**

**Register**

**Login**

**Logout**

**Password Recovery**

**OAuth Callback**

**\* Required fields.**

**\* Allowed values.**

**\* Identifier formats.**

**\* Request size where appropriate.**

**\* User permissions.**

**\* Test availability.**

**\* Feature structure for ML requests.**



**Invalid requests will receive safe error responses without exposing internal implementation details.**



**### 13.16 API Error Handling**



**The backend will use consistent error responses.**



**Errors will provide enough information for the frontend to respond appropriately without revealing:**



**\* Database credentials.**

**\* Internal file paths.**

**\* Stack traces.**

**\* Authentication secrets.**

**\* Internal infrastructure details.**



**Detailed diagnostic information will remain in appropriate server-side logs.**



**### 13.17 API Rate Limiting**



**Rate limiting will be considered for sensitive and resource-intensive endpoints.**



**Particular attention will be given to:**



**\* Authentication endpoints.**

**\* Test-start endpoints.**

**\* Traffic-processing endpoints.**

**\* ML inference endpoints.**

**\* Administrative endpoints.**



**The exact limits will be determined during implementation and performance testing.**



**### 13.18 CORS and Browser Security**



**The backend will configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing according to the deployed frontend origin.**



**Broad wildcard access will not be used unnecessarily in production.**



**HTTPS will be required for production communication between the frontend and backend.**



**### 13.19 API Documentation**

**\* Endpoint purpose.**

**\* Response format.**

**\* Authentication requirements.**

**\* Authorization requirements.**

**\* Error conditions.**



**Sensitive credentials and secrets will never appear in API documentation.**



**### 13.20 Backend Auditability**



**Important backend events will be recorded where appropriate.**



**Potential events include:**



**\* Login attempts.**

**\* Authorization failures.**

**\* Test creation.**

**\* Test execution.**
